newsitem.title: USA: Orange County judge refuses to end bankruptcy case.
newsitem.headline: Orange County judge refuses to end bankruptcy case.

text.p: An Orange County, California judge on Thursday refused to dismiss bankruptcy-related charges against the county's former assistant treasurer, Matthew Raabe.
In a victory for the prosecution, Superior Court Judge Everett Dickey rejected the defense motion, allowing the Raabe trial to move forward.
The defense was now expected to begin presenting its case on Monday.
Earlier this week, defense attorneys asked the court to dismiss the indictment against Raabe, whose long-awaited trial got underway in March.

The prosecution, which rested its case last week, has alleged that Raabe helped to divert nearly $90 million in interest earnings owed to cities, schools and special districts that were invested in the county-run portfolio.
In their motion to dismiss, Raabe's attorneys argued that the fund diversions were not illegal because the county had the right to set investment pool returns.
But the judge ruled on Thursday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence to send the case to the jury.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
Raabe, who faces up to 12 years in prison, was one of several Orange County officials to face charges following the bankruptcy. His trial was expected to last into May.

In April 1995, former Orange County Treasurer Robert Citron pleaded guilty to six felonies for his role in the crisis. A judge last November ordered him to spend a year in jail and pay a $100,000 fine, but Citron was later assigned to a community work program instead of jail.
Citron claimed that Raabe was the "mastermind" behind the scheme to divert the interest earnings.
Last October, a judge sentenced former Orange County budget director Ronald Rubino to probation for charges stemming from the investment crisis.
